note: Final lesson notes of course #1 (CCAO-F), music credits removed. Frozen: never edited; a later snapshot is v2.

lessons.title: What the Claude Certified Associate certifies, and how the exam works
objectives: Explain what the Claude Certified Associate proves and who it's for.
Describe how the exam is built and scored: 60 items, 120 minutes, 720 of 1,000, seven weighted domains.
Turn the official blueprint into a study map with Claude, and check it against the source.

lessons.title: The AI Fluency 4D framework
objectives: Name the four Ds and say what each one means.
Explain the two loops that connect them, and where each D lands on the exam.
Use all four on a real task in Claude: hand over, describe, check, and own the result.

lessons.title: Claude Desktop tour
objectives: Find your way around Claude Desktop: Chat, Cowork, Code and Settings.
Say in one line what each main tool does and where it lives.
Run your first chat, and switch models when the job changes.

lessons.title: The four decisions before the first prompt
objectives: Name the four decisions you make before the first prompt: entry point, features, model and context.
Explain why they set the ceiling on what a prompt can do, and where each one sits on the exam.
Run a real task through all four, out loud, and check the result.

lessons.title: Picking the right feature
objectives: Explain what each feature is for, and where it falls short.
Route any task with four questions.
Pick and combine features on a real job, then check the result.

lessons.title: Haiku, Sonnet, Opus
objectives: Tell Haiku, Sonnet and Opus apart: what each tier trades in capability, speed and cost.
Match a model, and its effort, to a job's cost, speed, quality and volume.
Run the same real job on all three and pick the right one from the evidence.

lessons.title: Context limits and memory
objectives: Explain what a context window is, and what happens when a chat gets long.
Decide when to keep going, restart, summarize, or persist.
Hand a working chat to a fresh one, and choose what Claude remembers.

lessons.title: Anatomy of an effective prompt
objectives: Name the six parts of an effective prompt and the question each one answers.
Rebuild a vague prompt into a complete one, for a business task and a technical task.
Spot which missing part caused a weak answer, and fix that part.

lessons.title: Task decomposition
objectives: Explain task decomposition and prompt chaining, and how each step's output feeds the next.
Split a real request into a short chain, with a checkpoint between steps.
Decide when to split, and when one prompt (and Claude's own thinking) is enough.

lessons.title: Iterating diagnostically
objectives: Read an answer against your success criteria, and name the symptom and its cause.
Change one thing per run, re-run, and tell whether that change fixed it.
Choose between editing the prompt, following up, and starting fresh.

lessons.title: Strategy by task type: analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming
objectives: Tell the four task types apart by what good looks like for each.
Adapt the prompt, and pick the feature, for analysis, research, drafting and brainstorming.
Judge each kind of output by its own test.

lessons.title: Discernment: checking accuracy and completeness against the source and the brief
objectives: Tell accuracy from completeness, and check each against the right reference.
Trace every claim to the source, and tick every requirement in the brief.
Turn what you find into one precise fix, and re-check only what changed.

lessons.title: Hallucinations: fabricated citations, numbers, quotes, and why confidence is not evidence
objectives: Explain what a hallucination is, and why fluent text can still be invented.
Spot the risky specifics (citations, numbers, quotes) and check each one against the source.
Set up a request so a gap gets admitted, not filled.

lessons.title: Inconsistencies and bias: catching contradictions and skewed framing
objectives: Spot inconsistencies: inside one answer, between answers, and against your source.
Recognize skewed framing, even when every fact is right.
Run the flip test, then ask for a fair answer when you need one.
